_note: Generic error types organized as an inspection walkthrough. These apply to any coin from any country. The order is deliberate: whole-coin checks first (cheapest to rule out), then zone-by-zone under magnification.

critical_lesson.title: Machine Doubling vs. a True Doubled Die
critical_lesson.why: This is the single most common mistake in error collecting. Machine doubling is worthless. A true doubled die can be worth thousands. They look similar at low magnification.
machine_doubling: Flat and shelf-like, as if the letter was smeared sideways
The doubled part sits LOWER than the main device
Looks scraped or sheared, with no rounded contours
Often shiny on the flat shelf where metal was pushed
Happens during the strike, on individual coins - not repeatable
true_doubled_die: Both images are ROUNDED and fully formed, at the SAME height
Clear notching at the corners of letters and digits
The doubling has depth and its own distinct outline
Comes from the die itself, so every coin from that die shows it identically
critical_lesson.test: Tilt the coin under the microscope light. If the second image is a flat shiny shelf that disappears as you change the angle, it is machine doubling. If it stays as a distinct rounded raised element, it may be a real doubled die.

checks.label: Weigh it on a 0.01g scale
checks.detail: Enter the weight in this tool and it will compare against mint specs and flag wrong-planchet candidates. This is the most reliable single test you can do.

checks.label: Magnet test
checks.detail: Most US coins are non-magnetic. Exceptions: 1943 steel cents ARE magnetic. Many foreign coins are steel and magnetic by design. An unexpected magnetic response means wrong planchet.

checks.label: Measure the diameter with calipers
checks.detail: A coin struck outside the collar spreads wider than normal and has a thin, flat, unfinished rim.

checks.label: Is the design centered?
checks.detail: An off-center strike shows a blank crescent on one side with the design pushed toward the other. Value rises with how far off-center it is, but the DATE must still be visible to command a real premium.

checks.label: Is the coin round and complete?
checks.detail: A curved bite out of the edge is a clipped planchet. Check for the 'Blakesley effect' - the rim opposite the clip is weak or missing, which confirms it is genuine rather than post-mint damage.

checks.label: Does one side show a mirror image of the other?
checks.detail: A raised, normal design on one side and an incuse, mirror-image design on the other is a brockage - a genuinely dramatic error.

checks.label: Check die rotation
checks.detail: Hold the coin with the obverse upright, then flip it top-to-bottom. On US coins the reverse should also be upright (coin alignment is 180 degrees - flip vertically and it reads right). More than about 15 degrees off is a rotated die error.

checks.label: Inspect the edge all the way around
checks.detail: Check reeding for gaps, partial reeding, or a plain edge where reeding belongs. On Presidential dollars check for missing, doubled, or inverted edge lettering. Look for a visible copper stripe on clad coins - if it is missing, suspect a wrong planchet.

zones.name: Step 2 - Obverse: Date and Mint Mark (20x-40x)

checks.label: Doubling on the date
checks.detail: Look for notching at digit corners and rounded secondary images. Apply the machine-doubling test before getting excited.

checks.label: Repunched or overdate
checks.detail: On older coins (pre-1909 especially), look for one digit punched over another, or a digit visible under the final date.

checks.label: Repunched mint mark (RPM)
checks.detail: Look for a second, offset outline of the mint mark. On coins before 1990 the mint mark was punched into each die by hand, so RPMs are common and collectible.

checks.label: Over mint mark (OMM)
checks.detail: One mint mark punched over a different letter - a D over an S, for example. Look for foreign curves or stems inside or beside the primary letter.

checks.label: Missing mint mark
checks.detail: Check whether the coin should have one. If the spot is smooth and undisturbed, it may be a genuine missing-mint-mark error. If it is scratched or dented, someone removed it.

checks.label: Doubling on LIBERTY and the motto
checks.detail: Check every letter for notched corners and split serifs. Doubled dies usually show strongest on one part of the design, not uniformly.

checks.label: Die cracks
checks.detail: Raised irregular lines wandering across the surface, often from rim to device. Metal flowed into a crack in the die.

checks.label: Cuds and die breaks
checks.detail: A cud is a raised blob of blank metal at the rim where a piece broke off the die entirely. Large cuds are quite valuable.

checks.label: Die clash marks
checks.detail: Faint ghost images of the OPPOSITE side's design showing through, caused by the dies striking each other with no planchet between them.

checks.label: Struck-through debris
checks.detail: An incuse impression of something that was on the planchet during the strike - grease (soft mushy missing detail), cloth (a weave pattern), wire, or a staple. A retained struck-through object still embedded in the coin is worth much more.

checks.label: Doubling on reverse lettering
checks.detail: Work systematically around the legend. Doubled die reverses are often overlooked because collectors focus on the obverse.

checks.label: Designer initials present and correct
checks.detail: Missing initials (like the 1982 No FG Kennedy half) happen when a die is over-polished.

checks.label: Die cracks, cuds, and gouges
checks.detail: Same as the obverse. Raised lines and blobs are die problems; incuse scratches are usually just damage.

checks.label: Lamination flaws
checks.detail: A layer of metal peeling, flaking, or having split away, caused by impurities or gas trapped in the planchet. Common on war nickels and clad coins.

checks.label: Missing clad layer
checks.detail: One side looks solid copper while the other looks normal, and the coin weighs noticeably light. A real and collectible error.

checks.label: Ruled out post-mint damage
checks.detail: The critical question for every suspected error: could this have happened AFTER the coin left the mint? Mint errors are almost always RAISED (metal flowed into a die flaw) or involve missing/displaced metal from the striking process. Post-mint damage is usually INCUSE - dents, scratches, gouges pushed INTO the surface - and displaces metal outward with a raised lip around it. Acid-etched, hammered, sanded, and machine-tooled coins fool a lot of people.

checks.label: Compared side by side with a normal example
checks.detail: Always have a known-normal coin of the same year and mint under the scope next to the suspect. Most 'errors' evaporate at this step, and it is the fastest way to build your eye.

checks.label: Worth submitting for authentication?
checks.detail: Grading costs roughly 20 to 40 dollars per coin plus shipping. It is worth it if the coin is plausibly worth 150 dollars or more, or if you need certainty to sell it. PCGS, NGC, and ANACS all attribute errors; ANACS is generally the cheapest and is well regarded for error attribution.

damage_not_error.title: Commonly Mistaken for Errors (these are NOT errors)

items.name: Machine doubling
items.why: Flat shelf-like doubling from die bounce. Extremely common. Worth nothing extra.

items.name: Die deterioration doubling
items.why: Mushy, distorted lettering from a worn-out die. Includes the 1955 'Poor Man's Doubled Die'.

items.name: Post-mint damage (PMD)
items.why: Dents, scratches, and gouges made after striking. Incuse with raised displaced metal at the edges.

items.name: Environmental damage
items.why: Corrosion, pitting, and acid etching. Often mistaken for lamination or struck-through.

items.name: Coins struck for magic/novelty
items.why: Two-headed coins, hollowed coins, and elongated pennies are made outside the mint.

items.name: Plated or coated coins
items.why: Gold-plated or chrome-plated coins are aftermarket. A plated cent will be over spec weight.

items.name: Wear-caused weak strikes
items.why: A worn coin loses detail evenly. A struck-through or filled die loses it in one specific area with sharp boundaries.

items.name: Vending machine / counting machine marks
items.why: Parallel scrapes and rim dings from mechanical handling.
